# Intro
It's been a long time coming but I've finally decided to take a look at [marimo](https://marimo.io/). For those of you who have not come across `marimo` before, it is a `python` notebook - kind of similar to `juptyer` notebooks - but with some great advantages. Notably, it is able to:

- reactively update when dependencies change. This is great for reproducibility and all-round conveniance - if I change something at the top of my notebook, the rest of the notebook just updates. No more running cells chunk by chunk.

- store files as simple text - unlike `juptyer` which produces kind of messy JSON. This enables `marimo` to [work well with version control](https://marimo.io/features/user-ml#git-is-much-clearer-in-marimo). This feature is historically what drew me to `quarto`. However, unlike `quarto`, `marimo` notebooks can also be used as standalone `python` scripts and serve as imports to other `python` scripts. 

- give access to built in widgets, which makes managing projects more streamlined and less reliant on imports. 

In today's post, I play around with the capabilities of `marimo` by loading in some data on Spanish verbs and conjugations. Since my website is built using `quarto` (and I use `quarto` in my day-to-day), I've installed the `marimo-quarto` extension. This can be done by running `quarto install extension marimo-team/quarto-marimo`. For more information about setting things up, the [official marimo docs](https://docs.marimo.io/guides/exporting/quarto/) are helpful.

And with that background covered, onto using `marimo` to make something!

::: {.callout}
Claude code was used in the development of the final conjugation tool, to enable me to very quickly explore the capabilities of `marimo` and make something actually useful that I probably couldn't at this stage. All writing is in my own words.
:::


# I'm trying to learn Spanish!
I've been trying to learn spanish for a long time, and have only recently pushed myself to start lessons. My lessons have lots of homework that require me to write sentences about my day, and specifically understand word conjugations. I'm (very) slowly getting the hang of it, but any tool that I can use to quickly look things up would be useful. I'll try and make one here, using marimo. 

### Conjugations 
Conjugation has always been a word that I've pretended to understand, and I only really know what it means now it's relevant to my day-to-day. For those who are like me and have no idea, a conjugation is how a verb changes its spelling to convey additional bits of information. In English, this may be demonstrated by the word "speak". It has various forms, such as spoke, spoken, speaks. In Spanish, conjugations are a whole new ball game, with many more different forms. It's common, and certainly my experience, that conjugations make Spanish quite difficult to learn. 

### Making a Conjugation Tool
My goal with this current project is to make a tool that makes it easy for me to look up a word and find its conjugations. My key aims:

- It needs to be accurate. 
- It needs to be fast. This is one reason I was keen to try out `marimo`
- It needs to be simple and consistent. 

#### It needs to be accurate
Luckily I'm not the first person to try and learn Spanish, and many great resources already exist that provide accurate data that I can use as lookups. Wiktionary (via https://kaikki.org/) is an excellent source of information on Spanish language, and includes a wealth of data on the conjugations as well as the etymology. I pulled the 1000 most common verbs (drawn from [FrequencyWords by Hermit Dave](https://github.com/hermitdave/FrequencyWords/blob/master/content/2018/es/es_50k.txt)) to make the example run more smoothly.

With this dataset, we can begin exploring the conjugations.

```{python .marimo}
#| echo: false
import json
import sys

import pandas as pd

VERBS_FILE = "spanish_verbs.json"

# Load the file. In the browser the cells run in Pyodide, which can only reach
# the file over HTTP, so fetch it from the site serving this page.
if sys.platform == "emscripten":
    from js import location
    from pyodide.http import pyfetch

    _url = f"{location.origin}/posts/marimo/{VERBS_FILE}"
    _response = await pyfetch(_url)
    if not _response.ok:
        raise RuntimeError(f"Couldn't load {_url} (HTTP {_response.status})")
    data = await _response.json()
else:
    data = json.loads((mo.notebook_dir() / VERBS_FILE).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))

# One row per verb; the nested conjugations and etymology stay in `data`.
verbs_df = (
    pd.DataFrame(data["verbs"])
    .assign(meaning=lambda d: d["glosses"].str[0])
    .loc[
        :,
        [
            "rank",
            "infinitive",
            "meaning",
            "ipa",
            "irregular",
            "gerund",
            "past_participle",
        ],
    ]
    .rename(
        columns={
            "rank": "Rank",
            "infinitive": "Verb",
            "meaning": "Meaning",
            "ipa": "Pronunciation",
            "irregular": "Irregular",
            "gerund": "Gerund",
            "past_participle": "Past participle",
        }
    )
)
```

#### It needs to be simple and consistent

Any tool I build needs to be simple, because conjugations in Spanish are so complex - things are hard enough already. 

##### Types of Conjugation
A Spanish verb changes its ending to show who is doing something (the *person*) and when or how it happens (the *tense* and *mood*). I found the [Spanish Language Tutor](https://youtu.be/FRV9fvWjMHA?si=AljiKHJo_7orl4f8) and [Ella Verbs](https://ellaverbs.com/resources/spanish-verb-tenses-in-english/)  helpful references here. Spanish has manyyy tenses spread across three moods (indicative, subjunctive, imperative). To keep it simple and to scaffold my learning appropriately, the tool below will conjugate the nine simple tenses that [Wiktionary](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Appendix:Spanish_verbs#) lists for every verb. Specifically I adapt a method from the [Spanish Language Tutor](https://youtu.be/FRV9fvWjMHA?si=AljiKHJo_7orl4f8) where the singular and plural versions are split into a 2 X 3 grid - this approach makes it easier to remember how things line up. 

| | Singular | Plural |
|---|---|---|
| **1st person** | yo (I) | nosotros / nosotras (we) |
| **2nd person** | tú (you, one person, informal) | vosotros / vosotras (you, more than one person, informal; mostly used in Spain) |
| **3rd person** | él / ella / usted (he, she, or *you* when being formal with one person) | ellos / ellas / ustedes (they, or *you* for more than one person) |

Note that *Usted* and *ustedes* mean "you" but take the third-person form, so *usted habla* is "you speak".

While the grid itself is simple, there are *9* different versions that it can take depending on the tense and mood of the sentence. Luckily, with `marimo`, we have the capacbilities to quickly switch between the 9 different version. The tool below also has a **Tenses and moods** tab that lists the nine tenses by mood, with an example of when to use each one.

```{=html}
<script>
  // Quarto opens site search on "f", "s" or "/" unless a form field has focus,
  // but marimo's inputs sit in a shadow DOM, so Quarto only sees the wrapper
  // element. Stop key presses in any form field reaching its listener on
  // document.
  document.body.addEventListener("keyup", (event) => {
    const el = event.composedPath()[0];
    if (el instanceof Element && (el.matches("input, select, textarea") || el.isContentEditable)) {
      event.stopPropagation();
    }
  });
</script>
```

```{python .marimo}
#| echo: false
word = mo.ui.dropdown(
    options=list(verb_lookup),
    value="hablar",
    searchable=True,
    label="Spanish verb",
)
tense = mo.ui.dropdown(
    options={labels["en"]: key for key, labels in data["meta"]["tenses"].items()},
    value="Present",
    label="Tense",
)
# The tabs only pick what to show; the content is drawn beneath them by a later
# cell. Defining them here, apart from anything that reads the verb, means
# picking a new verb doesn't rebuild them and reset the selected tab.
tabs = mo.ui.tabs(
    {"Conjugations": "", "Etymology": "", "Tenses and moods": "", "Common verbs": ""}
)
```

```{python .marimo}
#| echo: false
_verb = verb_lookup.get(word.value)

if _verb is None:
    _output = mo.md("Pick a verb above to see its conjugations.")
else:
    _forms = _verb["conjugations"][tense.value]
    _persons = data["meta"]["persons"]

    def _cell(person):
        return mo.stat(_forms.get(person, "—"), label=_persons[person], bordered=True)

    # Singular on the left, plural on the right, as in most textbooks.
    _grid = mo.vstack(
        [
            mo.hstack([_cell(singular), _cell(plural)], widths="equal")
            for singular, plural in [
                ("yo", "nosotros"),
                ("tu", "vosotros"),
                ("el", "ellos"),
            ]
        ]
    )
    _header = mo.md(
        f"### {_verb['infinitive']} {'(irregular)' if _verb['irregular'] else ''}\n\n"
        f"{_verb['glosses'][0]}. "
        f"Gerund *{_verb['gerund']}*, past participle *{_verb['past_participle']}*."
    )
    _output = mo.vstack([tense, _header, _grid])

conjugation_view = _output
```

##### Etymology
Wiktionary also records where each verb came from. For verbs inherited from Latin, the Latin entry lists its descendants across the Romance languages (and the odd English borrowing), which makes a family tree of related words. The **Etymology** tab shows that tree for the verb you pick, with its own branch highlighted. This is sometimes incredibly helpful, as some words share pretty close similarities with English and can be a nicer aid to memory. For example hablo (to speak) comes from the latin fabulari - which is the root of the english word fable (a story). While not the same, we can see the similarities. 



```{python .marimo}
#| echo: false
from html import escape

ROW, COL, PAD = 30, 220, 16
ACCENT = "#3987e5"


def etymology_tree(verb):
    """The verb's Latin cognate tree, or failing that its line of ancestors."""
    if verb["cognates"]:
        return verb["cognates"]
    if not verb["ancestors"]:
        return None
    node = {"lang": "Spanish", "code": "es", "word": verb["infinitive"], "children": []}
    for ancestor in verb["ancestors"]:  # newest first, so build from the verb upwards
        node["borrowed"] = ancestor["relation"] in ("borrowed", "learned borrowing")
        node = {**ancestor, "children": [node]}
    return node


def _without_groups(node):
    # Grouping nodes ("Ibero-Romance") have no word; lift their children up a
    # level to keep the tree narrow.
    children = []
    for child in node.get("children", []):
        child = _without_groups(child)
        children.extend(child["children"] if child["word"] is None else [child])
    return {**node, "children": children}


def etymology_svg(verb):
    tree = _without_groups(etymology_tree(verb))
    placed = []
    next_row = 0

    def place(node, depth):
        nonlocal next_row
        child_ids = [place(child, depth + 1) for child in node["children"]]
        if child_ids:
            row = (placed[child_ids[0]]["row"] + placed[child_ids[-1]]["row"]) / 2
        else:
            row, next_row = next_row, next_row + 1
        is_target = node["code"] == "es" and node["word"] == verb["infinitive"]
        placed.append(
            {
                "node": node,
                "row": row,
                "x": PAD + depth * COL,
                "y": PAD + 20 + row * ROW,
                "children": child_ids,
                "target": is_target,
                "on_path": is_target or any(placed[i]["on_path"] for i in child_ids),
            }
        )
        return len(placed) - 1

    place(tree, 0)

    # Each parent gets one trunk out to a spine, then a branch to each child,
    # so a borrowed (dashed) branch never runs over a shared trunk.
    edges = []
    for p in placed:
        if not p["children"]:
            continue
        spine = p["x"] + COL - 20
        edges.append((p["on_path"], f"M{p['x']},{p['y']} H{spine}", False))
        for c in (placed[i] for i in p["children"]):
            edges.append(
                (
                    c["on_path"],
                    f"M{spine},{p['y']} V{c['y']} H{c['x']}",
                    c["node"].get("borrowed"),
                )
            )

    parts = []
    # Highlighted edges last, so they sit on top.
    for on_path, d, borrowed in sorted(edges, key=lambda e: e[0]):
        stroke = (
            f'stroke="{ACCENT}" stroke-width="2.5"'
            if on_path
            else 'stroke="currentColor" stroke-opacity="0.35" stroke-width="1.5"'
        )
        dash = ' stroke-dasharray="5 4"' if borrowed else ""
        parts.append(f'<path d="{d}" fill="none" {stroke}{dash}/>')
    for p in placed:
        n = p["node"]
        word, lang = escape(n["word"]), escape(n["lang"])
        tip = f"{lang}: {word}" + (" (borrowed)" if n.get("borrowed") else "")
        fill = (
            f'fill="{ACCENT}"'
            if p["on_path"]
            else 'fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.55"'
        )
        parts.append(
            f'<circle cx="{p["x"]}" cy="{p["y"]}" r="{6 if p["target"] else 4}" {fill}><title>{tip}</title></circle>'
        )
        weight = "700" if p["target"] else "400"
        # Leaves are labelled beside the node; parents above their trunk,
        # clear of the edges to their children.
        x, y = (p["x"] + 8, p["y"] - 7) if p["children"] else (p["x"] + 10, p["y"] + 4)
        parts.append(
            f'<text x="{x}" y="{y}" font-size="13">'
            f'<tspan font-weight="{weight}">{word}</tspan>'
            f'<tspan dx="6" font-size="11" fill-opacity="0.65">{lang}</tspan></text>'
        )
    width = max(p["x"] for p in placed) + 260
    height = PAD * 2 + 20 + (next_row - 1) * ROW + 20
    return (
        f'<svg viewBox="0 0 {width} {height}" width="{width}" style="max-width:100%;height:auto;color:var(--bs-body-color, inherit)" '
        f'fill="currentColor" font-family="inherit" role="img" '
        f'aria-label="Etymology tree for {escape(verb["infinitive"])}">{"".join(parts)}</svg>'
    )
```

```{python .marimo}
#| echo: false
_verb = verb_lookup.get(word.value)

if _verb is None:
    _output = mo.md("")
elif etymology_tree(_verb) is None:
    _output = mo.md(f"Wiktionary has no etymology for *{_verb['infinitive']}*.")
else:
    _scope = (
        "Other branches are related words in other languages."
        if _verb["cognates"]
        else "Wiktionary lists no Latin descendants for this verb, so this shows its line of ancestors only."
    )
    _output = mo.vstack(
        [
            mo.md(f"#### Where *{_verb['infinitive']}* comes from"),
            mo.Html(etymology_svg(_verb)),
            mo.md(
                f"The highlighted path leads to *{_verb['infinitive']}*. Solid lines are inherited words, "
                f"dashed lines are borrowings. {_scope}\n\n"
                "> " + (_verb["etymology_text"] or "").replace("\n", "\n> ") + "\n\n"
                "Source: Wiktionary via [Kaikki.org](https://kaikki.org/) (CC BY-SA 4.0)."
            ),
        ]
    )

etymology_view = _output
```

```{python .marimo}
#| echo: false
tenses_view = mo.md(
    """
| Tense | Spanish name | Used for | Example |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Present | presente | current situations, habits, general truths | *Hablo* español. (I speak Spanish.) |
| Preterite | pretérito indefinido, also called pretérito perfecto simple | actions completed at a specific time | Ayer *hablé* con ella. (I spoke to her yesterday.) |
| Imperfect | pretérito imperfecto | habits, descriptions and ongoing actions in the past, "used to" | De niño *hablaba* francés. (As a child I used to speak French.) |
| Future | futuro simple | future actions, and guesses about the present | Mañana *hablaré* con él. (I'll speak to him tomorrow.) |
| Conditional | condicional simple | hypotheticals, polite requests, wishes | *Hablaría* más si tuviera tiempo. (I'd speak more if I had time.) |
| Present subjunctive | presente de subjuntivo | doubt, wishes, feelings and uncertainty about the present or future | Quiero que *hables* más despacio. (I want you to speak more slowly.) |
| Imperfect subjunctive | pretérito imperfecto de subjuntivo | the same uses in the past, and "if" clauses about unlikely situations | Si *hablara* mejor, viajaría más. (If I spoke better, I'd travel more.) |
| Imperative | imperativo afirmativo | commands and instructions | ¡*Habla* más alto! (Speak up!) |
| Negative imperative | imperativo negativo | telling someone not to do something, using *no* with the present subjunctive | ¡No *hables*! (Don't speak!) |

There is no *yo* command, so in the imperatives that card shows a dash.

Descriptions adapted from [Ella Verbs](https://ellaverbs.com/resources/spanish-verb-tenses-in-english/).
"""
)
```
